bus_p3_r1: Your Protector (I know, almost the same name, but this one's the grown-up you) earns that protective part's trust mostly out in ordinary life. Over time, that part sees what you actually do and starts to believe a trustworthy adult has shown up. One kind talk in your head usually won't outweigh years of evidence the other way, and I don't think it should. The things you do can be small, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about. Or saying no to someone, and not texting an hour later to take it back. That second one can be really hard.
bus_p4_r1: That part doesn't have to leave first. You could even tell it, "Stay right there if you want." It can keep watch and still let you take one small step, as long as you're present and can stop. If it says no, that's a no. When it does let you go on, follow whatever changes. A critic that kept saying "This is stupid" might soften into "I'm scared to get my hopes up." That one's easier to be kind to.
bus_p5_r1: No need to restart the whole exercise and go looking for your little one again, like they're hiding behind the couch. A vague hurt can turn into something clearer, like wanting someone on your side for once. If it does, try being that someone. You could even say it out loud: "I'm on your side." It may feel silly to say out loud. Notice how it lands anyway. You don't need to know how old you were, or what happened, to do that. A small shift counts, and more intensity isn't the only way forward. Sometimes all that happens is your shoulders come down a little.
